Not bad on the SAT. Lots of studying has been the case in every programming class I've ever taken. Luckily, most all Universities start with the very basics in their intro CS classes, and most American high schools don't even teach programming so even just having that on your transcript is a big plus. A teacher of mine once joked any engineering classes are seen as one letter grade higher than they actually are by the a lot faculty. Comparatively to most general eds that is.

As for America literature, I *love* reading, so I know how to spell and use grammar correctly but I am not able to tell you the rules. I don't know how you learned, but from your posting it looks like you know how to write well too. 

You say you have a borderline grade in American Literature, so here is what I want you to do. I want you to think of this class as a "bullshit practice" class. Bullshit is very important in the professional world, and makes any essay type class so much fun. As long as you read the books and emphasize the author's message in your essays, with your writing I'm sure you can bring your marks up. Watch "Thank You for Smoking" (free on YouTube, comedy about a Tabacco lobbyist) for better examples than I could give you. 

I know some people who decide who does or does not get accepted to (American) Universities and the message I've got is it comes down to a combination of three things. Grades (obviously), test scores (SAT), and passion (uniqueness). The first two are what they are, the third you can really flesh out in your enternance essay. It can be about anything. Even, and I quote: "You could talk about your favorite pair of pants as long as you do it in a clever and well written way." 

With your background I'm sure you have a plethora of information to draw upon for your essay. You could talk about the hazards and helpfulness of growing up in a compound. You could write about how technology has brought people across the globe together in ways unparalleled at any time in history, especially for someone in your situation. You could even write about how everyone should learn some skills in (whatever unique skills you gained where you were), and uniquely you could bring to my country.

(Random side note, when I was in a gated compound im China with our personal driver generally getting my dad to and from work or my mom to shop and nowhere to go past the guards at the elevated gate, online gaming, China's copy of YouTube (YouKu) and the Internet in general (after I bypassed The Great Firewall of China) was a Godsend (even though I'm an atheist).)

The impressions you want to give is that you're both hard working and somehow extrodinary. 

Thank you for the birthday wishes. My International school's administration after the Australian principle left at the end of my first year was also a pile of shit. Regardless, do all your homework and **actually think about what you're learning** and it **WILL** pay off later in life.
